summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.9% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 28.0% in the prior period, placing the sector in the measurable middle range of adoption across the economy. That figure covers firms of all sizes and all subsets of the sector, from residential brokerages to large commercial landlords, so it masks considerable variation in how deeply AI is embedded in any given operation.

The most established use of AI in real estate is automated valuation. Zillow publishes Zestimate home valuations for more than 110 million homes using a neural network model trained on county and tax assessor records, MLS feeds, listing signals, and historical sales data, with updates running multiple times per week. HouseCanary similarly offers AI-powered valuations and forecasts covering more than 136 million U.S. properties, combining machine learning with image recognition technology that assesses home condition directly from photos. Opendoor takes valuation a step further by using pricing models to make direct purchase offers to sellers, putting real balance-sheet exposure behind its algorithms. These consumer and institutional valuation tools represent nearly two decades of production machine learning in the sector.

That maturity has attracted federal oversight. The FHFA, CFPB, OCC, Federal Reserve Board, FDIC, and NCUA jointly finalized quality control standards for automated valuation models used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers in determining the collateral worth of a consumer's principal dwelling. Under the rule, institutions must adopt policies, practices, procedures, and control systems to ensure AVMs adhere to standards designed to maintain a high level of confidence in estimates, protect against data manipulation, avoid conflicts of interest, and require random sample testing and reviews. This is the first binding federal framework specifically targeting the sector's core AI, and it applies at the point where valuation models affect mortgage credit decisions.

Beyond valuation, AI is spreading through leasing and building operations. EliseAI offers an agentic conversational platform that handles messages, calls, and tasks automatically around the clock, scheduling tours, following up with prospects, and managing maintenance requests without human involvement at each step. Prophia uses AI to extract key lease terms from commercial real estate documents and combines that extraction with expert validation to produce structured lease data for owners and operators. Building Engines, a JLL company, offers an AI-powered property management platform called Prism that delivers answers, recommendations, and automation aimed at cutting costs and growing net operating income. Matterport digitizes physical space through 3D capture and computer vision, enabling virtual tours, floor plans, and portfolio-wide management decisions from a central platform. JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, deploying it across brokerage, facilities management, and portfolio analytics.

The investment and startup ecosystem around these tools is organized and active. CRETI, the Center for Real Estate Technology and Innovation, maintains a network of over 500 investors focused on real estate technology and runs a zero-equity accelerator for emerging proptech companies. NAR REACH, created by Second Century Ventures, describes itself as the most active venture fund in the global real estate technology space and serves as the National Association of Realtors' vehicle for vetting and scaling residential proptech. CREtech convenes commercial real estate leaders specifically around AI deployment, with its New York conference drawing 3,000 leaders and facilitating over 20,000 pre-scheduled meetings.

A reader considering deployment should note that the clearest ROI evidence in the sources centers on automation of repetitive, document-heavy tasks, specifically lease abstraction, tenant communications, and property valuation, where AI replaces time-consuming manual work with structured outputs. The regulatory risk is most concentrated in valuation: any institution using AVMs in mortgage origination or securitization is now subject to the interagency quality control rule, which requires documented governance, testing, and conflict-of-interest controls. For operational AI in leasing and building management, the sources point to cost reduction and productivity gains as the primary case, though specific quantified figures are not provided in the available material. The sector's adoption trend is moving upward, the vendor landscape is well-populated, and the regulatory framework for the highest-stakes application is already in place.
